The study was conducted in two phases: a Task I preliminary design analysis and a Task I final design analysis.
Eight air-cooled turbine blade designs in 0.75-in. (0.01905 m), 1.0-in. (0.0254 m), and 1.5-in. (0.0381 m) chord sizes were investigated in the preliminary design phase.
A pin fin convection-cooled configuration and a film-impingement-cooled configuration were selected for the final design analysis.
The final design analysis determined the allowable turbine inlet temperature as a function of cooling air inlet temperature and turbine inlet total pressure for each chord size.
The final design analysis also determined the minimum cooling flow required as a function of cooling air inlet temperature with a constant turbine inlet temperature for each chord size.

The preliminary analysis showed that allowable turbine inlet temperature increases with increasing chord for the convection-cooled and transpiration-cooled designs, but the film-convection-cooled designs did not have a significant change in turbine inlet temperature with chord.
The film-convection-cooled designs allowed turbine inlet temperatures about 200°F (111°K) higher than the convection-cooled designs.
Transpiration cooling offered an advantage only for the 1.5-in. (0.0381 m) chord size.
Turbine inlet total pressure had relatively little effect on turbine inlet temperature capability over the range studied.

Decreasing cooling air inlet temperature or increasing chord size reduced the cooling air flow required for the convection-cooled blade, but this trend was not as apparent in the film-convection-cooled design.
An estimated life of 1000 hr was obtained for each final design based on creep relaxation analysis or a maximum metal temperature limit.
Additional studies were performed on the effects of reducing cooling air inlet pressure and varying flow control orifice sizes.
The study was based on a constant blade span of 1.75 in. (0.04445 m) and assumed a life of 1000 hr for the IN-100 blade material.
The metal temperature distribution was calculated using a three-dimensional thermal analyzer computer program that considered spanwise and chordwise conduction and variable thermal conductivity.
Stress calculations accounted for centrifugal stresses, thermal stresses, and bending stresses due to thermal distortion.
